name: Spotlight effect
statement: People think others notice them about twice as much as others do, so an embarrassing shirt or a stumbled sentence feels more public than it was.
meaning: The claim is about a gap between two quantities that can both be measured: how much attention you believe you are getting and how much you are actually getting. Because your own appearance and behaviour are the most available thing in your own head, you start from that vivid impression and adjust downward for the fact that others have their own concerns. The adjustment is too small, which is anchoring applied to yourself. The design that makes this testable is the one that measures both sides in the same room at the same time.

origin.who: Thomas Gilovich, Victoria Husted Medvec and Kenneth Savitsky
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Their paper is "The spotlight effect in social judgment: An egocentric bias in estimates of the salience of one's own actions and appearance", it gave the phenomenon its name, and it opens by placing itself where Ross and Sicoly's work on responsibility allocation left off.

evidence: Five studies, in three paradigms, all reported in the 2000 paper. Study 1 ran 109 Cornell undergraduates: 15 wore the shirt, 64 watched in sessions of two to six, and 30 were controls who saw a videotaped reenactment instead. The shirt carried a 21 cm by 24 cm picture of Barry Manilow, chosen because pretest interviews suggested a majority of Cornell undergraduates would be embarrassed to wear it. The targets estimated that 46% of the room could name him and 23% of the observers could, which the authors call exactly twice. Per session the targets overshot by 23 points, 95% CI 9 to 38, and by 27 points, CI 11 to 43, once the sessions holding two and three observers are dropped. A one-way analysis of variance across the targets and the two control groups gave F(2, 42) = 5.76, p < .01, and the targets sat above the controls who had been told it was Manilow, t(42) = 3.07, p < .005, and above those who had not, t(42) = 2.66, p < .02. Estimates still tracked reality, r = .50, p < .05. A footnote reports men estimating 59% against women's 35%, t(13) = 1.92, p < .10, which the authors call marginal and possibly an anomaly. Study 2 ran 79 people, most of them Cornell undergraduates and the rest school pupils on Cornell's summer session. Its 15 targets picked a shirt they were pleased to wear, bearing Bob Marley, Jerry Seinfeld or Martin Luther King, Jr. They estimated 48% against an actual 8%, a per-session gap of 40 points, 95% CI 21 to 59. Study 3 moved from clothes to talk. It put 193 undergraduates into 42 groups of three to seven, had them discuss inner-city policy, then rank themselves as they thought the group would. Taking the group as the unit of analysis, they were wrong on all six dimensions, hardest on speech errors, where a predicted rank of 2.30 met an actual 2.96, t(41) = 6.84, p < .00001. The last two studies test the mechanism. Study 4 sent 44 Northwestern undergraduates into a room of confederates in a Vanilla Ice shirt, and of the 30 who named one alternative figure before settling, 23 named a higher one, binomial z = 2.74, p < .01. Study 5 gave some of 30 Northwestern undergraduates 15 minutes to get used to the Manilow shirt. They estimated 37% where those sent straight in estimated 51%, t(28) = 2.26, p < .05. Four further participants were run in Study 5 and discarded for confederate errors, so 30 is the analysed sample rather than the recruited one.

replication.headline: No repeat of the estimated-against-actual design was found, and the nearest recent study runs the paradigm in reverse with scent instead of a shirt.
replication.detail: Ozdem-Mertens, Meshi, Inchauspe and Tamir posted a preprint in 2022, not peer reviewed, that models its procedure on the 2000 studies. Targets chose a scent, were sprayed with it, and walked into a room of observers either at once or after a delay. In Study 1 they estimated that 21% of observers had noticed the scent where 64% had, F(1, 28) = 36.84, p < .001, partial eta squared .57, on 30 targets and 111 observers after preregistered exclusions. Study 2 found the same reversal on 58 targets, 24% estimated against 46% actual, F(1, 56) = 17.12, p < .001, partial eta squared .23. The 2000 paper predicts this for behaviour people have stopped noticing in themselves, and names smokers and heavy users of cologne as cases. So the preprint tests the account rather than repeating the T-shirt result, and the site does not count it as a replication.

limits: The search behind that verdict looked at PubMed, which holds ten records for the phrase and none of them a repeat, Europe PMC, Crossref titles, the OSF preprint index including PsyArXiv, and the 528 papers Semantic Scholar records as citing the 2000 article, scanned for replication wording. Web searches for classroom and undergraduate repeats of the T-shirt paradigm turned up two student-journal items whose full text a repository firewall would not serve, neither of which is described as running the estimated-against-actual design. That is a statement about what was found rather than proof that nothing exists, and this literature has no equivalent of the Many Labs projects to check against. The nearest published follow-up is Gilovich, Kruger and Medvec in 2002 on perceived variability, a different authorship from the 2000 trio, and it extends the idea rather than testing it again. The original studies also used small samples at three universities. Fifteen people wore the shirt in Study 1 and 15 in Study 2, the sessions ran with two to six observers each, and Study 5 analysed 30 of the 34 people it ran. The paper reports no standardised effect size. It gives 95% intervals on the overestimation itself, 9 to 38 percentage points in Study 1 and 21 to 59 in Study 2, which is what a future replication would have to be compared against.
misreadings: The effect is usually passed on as reassurance, that nobody is looking at you, which is stronger than the finding. Almost a quarter of the room did identify the shirt. What was measured is a gap between 46% and 23%, so the accurate summary is that people notice you about half as much as you think, not that they do not notice you. The effect is also routinely merged with the illusion of transparency, the belief that inner states are visible, which this site treats as its own entry. Gilovich, Medvec and Savitsky keep the two apart in their own discussion, as one bias about overt actions and appearance and a second about internal experience, sharing a mechanism and resting on separate experiments. The overclaiming of one's share of a joint effort is a third relative, covered here under egocentric bias.

sources.text: Gilovich, T., Medvec, V. H., & Savitsky, K. (2000). The spotlight effect in social judgment: An egocentric bias in estimates of the salience of one's own actions and appearance. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 78(2), 211-222.

Gilovich, T., & Savitsky, K. (1999). The spotlight effect and the illusion of transparency. Current Directions in Psychological Science, 8(6), 165-168. Cited for its existence and authorship, which were checked at Crossref; the full text could not be obtained for this entry.

Gilovich, T., Kruger, J., & Medvec, V. H. (2002). The spotlight effect revisited: Overestimating the manifest variability of our actions and appearance. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 38(1), 93-99. An extension, not a replication, and note that Kruger stands where Savitsky did in 2000.
Ozdem-Mertens, C., Meshi, D., Inchauspe, A., & Tamir, D. (2022). The reverse spotlight effect: Failing to notice what others notice about us. PsyArXiv preprint, not peer reviewed.
